sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know relative clauses with *que* and *quien* from B1 Unit 5 (*La amiga que vive al lado*, *el vecino con quien hablamos*). They add information about a person, a thing or a place without starting a new sentence. The Cold War is full of such descriptions: the superpowers, the blocs and the policies that divided them.

sections.title: Que and quien at work
rows: Estados Unidos, que defendía el capitalismo
the United States, which defended capitalism
la política que quería frenar el comunismo
the policy that wanted to halt communism
los países que veían una amenaza en el comunismo
the countries that saw a threat in communism
Truman, quien había llegado al cargo en 1945
Truman, who had come into office in 1945

items.spanish: La Unión Soviética, que defendía el comunismo, dirigía el otro bloque.
items.english: The Soviet Union, which defended communism, led the other bloc.

items.spanish: La OTAN es una alianza militar que unió en 1949 a Estados Unidos con varios países de Europa.
items.english: NATO is a military alliance that in 1949 united the United States with several European countries.

items.spanish: La contención fue una política que quería frenar el comunismo.
items.english: Containment was a policy that wanted to halt communism.

items.spanish: El presidente Truman, quien había llegado al cargo en 1945, prometió ayuda.
items.english: President Truman, who had come into office in 1945, promised help.

sections.content: *Que* does not change for gender or number: *la alianza que*, *los bloques que*. With a comma, the clause adds extra information (*Estados Unidos, que defendía el capitalismo, …*). Without a comma, it says which one you mean (*los países que veían una amenaza*). *Quien* is for people only, mostly after a comma or a preposition.
